title: God Remembered Rachel — Rivalry, Mandrakes, Flocks
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. The last lesson stopped on one sentence: "This time I will praise Yahweh." Those were the words of a woman who was not loved, spoken on the day her fourth child was born.
Today the camera swings across to the other side of the tent — to the woman who was loved. And what you will find is that the one who was loved had a despair of her own.
So let me put a question to you first. Have you ever demanded from a human being something that only God can give?
"You have to make me feel that I am worth something." "You have to make me feel safe." "You have to make my life mean something."

Let me put the answer at the very front: put a human being in God's chair and you will wound each other every time — the one being asked cannot supply it, and the one asking never receives it. And God's remembering nearly always comes after every human method has been used up.
1. Give Me Children, or Else I Will Die
Verse 1: "When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. She said to Jacob, 'Give me children, or else I will die.'"

Brothers and sisters, before anything else let me say something fair to her: her pain was real. In that culture, the shame carried by a woman who bore no children is something we can hardly imagine today. And she had to stand there and watch her sister bear one child after another.

"Envied" is וַתְּקַנֵּא (*vateqane*), and it is a fascinating word — when the very same word is used of God, it is rendered "jealous", the jealousy of a God who will not share what belongs to him. The heat is identical; only the direction is different.

And "I will die" is מֵתָה אָנֹכִי, literally "I am a dead woman." Brothers and sisters, you have heard that sentence before — in Genesis 25:32, Esau says, "Behold, I am about to die. What good is the birthright to me?"

The same construction. One of them for a bowl of stew, the other for a child. A person in extreme deprivation will always come out with "I am about to die" — and that sentence turns "now" into "everything."
Then verse 2: "Jacob's anger burned against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in God's place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?'"
The Hebrew behind "his anger burned" is וַיִּחַר־אַף (*vayichar-af*), and it says literally "his nose burned." He lost his temper.
But listen to what he actually said: "Am I in God's place?" הֲתַחַת אֱלֹהִים אָנֹכִי — "Am I standing in the position of God?"
Brothers and sisters, that is put with great precision. No human being can supply what only God can give.
And that sentence will come round once more in Genesis. In 50:19, Joseph says to the brothers who had done him harm, "Don't be afraid, for am I in the place of God?"
One sentence, two hearts. In chapter 30 it is a shrug — don't come to me, this is not my department. In chapter 50 it is reverence — the judgement seat is not mine, and I will not sit down in it.
Brothers and sisters, a perfectly correct sentence can be an escape or it can be a surrender. The difference lies in whether there is a God inside the person saying it.
Rachel says, "Give me children, or else I will die," and Jacob loses his temper. Was that the right response?

Jacob said, "Am I in God's place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?" What he said is theologically flawless, and his timing and his tone were completely wrong. A person desperate enough to say "or else I will die" does not need a lesson on the sovereignty of God. This passage is a very direct warning to us: right truth placed in the wrong moment turns into something that wounds. The practical order is this — catch the feeling first (I know how much this hurts, I am here with you), and handle the content afterwards, and hold the content back until the other person asks you for it. Truth does not expire because you said it a few days late; a person, though, will shut the door on you because you said a few sentences too early.
The pain of infertility comes up again and again in Scripture. How should we speak about it to people facing the same thing today?

First, we must be extremely careful never to turn "and then God gave her a child" into a formula. The reason the stories of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah were written down is precisely that they are exceptions on the line of God's saving work, not a general guarantee. Scripture also never puts an equals sign between bearing children and being blessed. So there are three things a pulpit ought to do: acknowledge that the pain is real; refuse to explain on God's behalf why it has not happened yet; and never press anyone with "if you had enough faith you would have one." And the most practical care looks like this: do not ask "when are you going to have a baby?" at family gatherings, do not pass on folk remedies with nothing behind them, and go with them as they carry what is in their hearts to God.
2. The Arms Race Between Two Sisters
Verse 3, Rachel says: "Behold, my maid Bilhah. Go in to her, that she may bear on my knees, and I also may obtain children by her."

"Bear on my knees" is עַל־בִּרְכַּי — the legal gesture of adoption in the ancient world. And "I also may obtain children" is אִבָּנֶה, literally "I may be built up" — בֵּן (son) and בָּנָה (to build) come from the same root.
Brothers and sisters, you have heard this sentence before, in chapter 16. Sarai said exactly the same thing in her day.
The third generation now. The same expedient, taken down off the shelf one more time.

And I want you to notice the verbs in verse 4 and in verse 9. Rachel "gave him Bilhah her servant as wife" — she took, וַתִּקַּח, and she gave, וַתִּתֵּן. By verse 9, Leah "took Zilpah, her servant, and gave her to Jacob as a wife" — the very same two verbs.
The younger sister makes a move; the older sister answers with the identical play. This is an arms race.

And those names are the scoreboard of the war. "Dan" — God has judged me. "Naphtali" — in the original, "I have wrestled with my sister with mighty wrestlings, and have prevailed." "Gad" — how fortunate. "Asher" — happy am I.
Brothers and sisters, four children, four names — and every one of them was said for the other woman to hear.

Then come verses 14 to 16, that most humiliating business with the mandrakes. Reuben found mandrakes out in the field — in those days people believed the plant helped a woman conceive. Rachel asked her sister for some, and Leah said, "Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son's mandrakes, also?"
And Rachel said, "Therefore he will lie with you tonight for your son's mandrakes."
Brothers and sisters, two sisters trading one night of a husband for a handful of herbs.
And the most ironic part of the whole affair comes afterwards: Rachel, who got the mandrakes, did not conceive; Leah, who handed them over, bore two more sons and a daughter.
The author does not need to say "the mandrakes did not work." He only has to record who bore children and who did not.
Two sisters bearing children through their servants, trading a husband for mandrakes — what is the Bible doing by recording all this?

It is letting us see what a household without order grows into. There is envy in this chapter, and comparison, and bargaining, and people used as instruments — and not once does God step out and say, "this is good." The twelve tribes of Israel were born inside a family like that. The text is not praising the process; it is showing us how low the starting point of grace can be. That carries two things for us. First, do not prettify the people in the Bible. Second, do not assume that because your own family is a shambles God cannot use you. The place where God works is very often not a model home.
3. A Light from the Original: God Remembered Rachel
Verse 22: "God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her, and opened her womb."
Brothers and sisters, "remembered" is וַיִּזְכֹּר (*vayizkor*) — you saw it back in chapter 8. "God remembered Noah" uses the identical word.
It does not mean "the thought came back to him." It means "he began to act on that person's behalf."
And I want you to notice the moment at which this sentence appears: it appears after every single method has been used up.
Servants bearing children — tried. Mandrakes — tried. The rivalry, the bargaining, the keeping of score — all of it tried.
And then the text says: God remembered Rachel.

Brothers and sisters, I am not saying that God waits for us to fail before he moves. I am saying this: as long as there is still a method in your hand, you will never really open that hand. And the moment the hand opens is usually the moment God goes to work.
Verse 23, she says, "God has taken away my reproach."

Look at the subject of that sentence. For twenty-odd verses the subject has been "I" — I want, I may be built up, I have wrestled, I have prevailed. Here, for the first time, the subject becomes "God."
And she names the child Joseph, saying, "May Yahweh add another son to me."
Brothers and sisters, that is a fascinating line. She has only just received, and already she is asking for the next one. The hole inside a human heart is not something one child can fill.
And that is the deepest lesson in this chapter: what she wanted was never only a child. What she wanted was the feeling of "I am enough." And there is only One who can give that.
"God remembered Rachel" — is that the same thing as "God remembered Noah" in chapter 8?

It is the same word (זָכַר), and it means the same thing: not the thought coming back, but action taken because of a covenant. Verse 22 says, "God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her, and opened her womb" — three actions in a row. And before that, the text has spent a full twenty verses on her rivalry, on her pain, on her own words about wrestling with her sister. So the remembering is not something that happened once she had behaved well enough; the text simply says that the time came, and God acted. That matters enormously for anyone who is waiting: seeing nothing move today does not mean you have been forgotten. Scripture's own wording is this — when he remembers, things begin.
Rachel names the boy Joseph and says, "May Yahweh add another son to me." Is that greed?

"Joseph" (יוֹסֵף) means precisely "he will add." The text does not rebuke her, and God did in fact give her one more son later on — only that time she paid for it with her own life (chapter 35). So when we read this line we need not rush to a verdict on whether she was greedy. We should see instead a very human fact: after receiving, a person still wants more. That in itself is not necessarily sin, but it is worth being alert to — because if our contentment is permanently located in the next thing, then no matter how much God gives, we will never stop to give thanks. The practical remedy is very simple: before you ask for something new, count once what you already have.
4. Rods, Flocks, and a Secret Nobody Said Out Loud
From verse 25 on, Jacob wants to go home. And Laban says, "I have divined that Yahweh has blessed me for your sake."

So the two of them negotiate wages. Jacob's terms are that the speckled, the spotted and the black among the flock should be his. And once Laban had agreed, "that day, he removed the male goats that were streaked and spotted … and gave them into the hand of his sons. He set three days' journey between himself and Jacob."
Brothers and sisters, Laban picked out everything that met the terms before anything else could happen. That is a calculation carried out in plain sight.

Then verses 37 to 43 give us that famous business with the rods. Jacob took fresh rods of poplar, almond and plane tree, peeled white streaks into them, and set them in the watering troughs where the flocks came to drink, so that the animals would see them while they were mating. And the flocks produced streaked and spotted young.
What is going on here? The folk belief of the day held that whatever a breeding animal looked at would shape the appearance of its young. Jacob in all likelihood believed that himself.

And now turn over to the next chapter. In Genesis 31:10 to 12 Jacob says, "During mating season, I lifted up my eyes, and saw in a dream, and behold, the male goats which leaped on the flock were streaked, speckled, and grizzled. The angel of God said to me in the dream … for I have seen all that Laban does to you."
Brothers and sisters, God tells him in a dream, in person: that was my doing.
The author's craft here is lovely. First he lets you watch the man's folk remedy, and then in the next chapter he lets God pull the curtain back.
So when verse 43 says, "The man increased exceedingly", that was not the achievement of the rods. It was the blessing of God.

And I want to say something here very plainly: blessing is not the same thing as approval. Jacob is still calculating all the way through this passage — verses 41 and 42 say that he used the method only on the stronger animals and left the feebler ones for Laban. God blessed him, and God also told him the truth in the very next chapter.
Jacob used rods to make the flocks bear spotted young. Is the Bible teaching us a technique that works?

No. Two things need noticing. First, the text only records what he did; it never says that this was the reason it worked. Second, in chapter 31 he lifts the lid on it himself: he says God showed him in a dream, and he says, "Thus God has taken away your father's livestock, and given them to me" — he credits God, not the rods. So the right reading is this: those rods were the folk practice of his day, and the One who actually made him prosper was God. That is intensely practical for us. Do not turn an incidental device inside a biblical narrative into a spiritual formula for today; and do not assume that because God once worked through some particular action, that action has become a rule we are obliged to copy.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "God remembered Rachel" as though God will give if only you hold out long enough. The point of this chapter is God's own initiative in remembering, not a result a person ground out by endurance. Preach it as a formula and everyone who has not yet received will conclude that they are not devout enough, not patient enough, not full enough of faith — and that is a very deep wound.

The second is turning the rods among the flock into some kind of spiritual technique. In chapter 31 Jacob himself says that God did it, in a dream. Preach it as a technique and the congregation will go chasing methods instead of chasing God. And today's rods come in a great many wrappers: a certain formula for prayer, a certain number, a certain way of phrasing a declaration.

The third is preaching Jacob's wealth as God's endorsement of his methods. Blessing is not approval. A good outcome does not make the process right. Blur the two together and your congregation will learn to use results as a guarantor for methods — "look, this way gets blessed too."

The fourth is taking the sisters' rivalry and using it to sneer at women. The disease in this chapter is Jacob's favouritism and the disorder of the whole household; it is not that "women are petty." Turn it into a joke about the sexes and you will hurt people, and you will lose the point entirely.

The fifth is lifting "Am I in God's place?" out of its setting and treating it as a stand-alone golden verse. In this chapter that sentence is what Jacob shrugs off in his anger — he says it and nothing follows: no praying together, no seeking God together. The same sentence does not grow into reverence until chapter 50. So when you quote it, say plainly which of the two you mean.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: comparison in a Chinese family covers everything — the children's marks, their jobs, their marriages, the grandchildren, the flat. I know perfectly well I should not compare, and yet every time the family gathers at New Year I come away hurt. What do I do? Brothers and sisters, this chapter is a documentary about family comparison. Let me give you three very practical directions. First, identify the scoreboard. Rachel and Leah kept score with the names of their children — and every one of those names was said for the other woman to hear. You have a scoreboard too: who is it that you most often measure yourself against on the inside? Write it down. Second, watch for that "I am about to die" construction. A person in a state of deprivation exaggerates: without this I am finished, without this I am worth nothing. The moment that sentence appears, it is a warning light. Third — and this is the crucial step — change who you are asking. Rachel asked Jacob for children, and Jacob could not supply them. Who is it that you are asking, "you have to affirm me"? If that person is your parent, your spouse or your boss, they probably cannot supply it either. Psalm 62:5 says, "My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him."

The second question: I have been praying for years about having a child, and people tell me that such-and-such a method works, that so-and-so's prayers are very effective. Should I go and try? Brothers and sisters, I want to handle this one very gently. First, the text has not one word of rebuke for Rachel's pain. Her longing was legitimate, and so is yours. Second, about methods: this chapter tells us plainly that the mandrakes did nothing — the one who got them did not conceive, and the one who gave them away did. And legitimate medical treatment is an entirely different thing from a superstitious folk remedy: the first is wisdom God has given to human beings, and you may use it; the second puts your hope onto an object that has no power in it. The way to tell them apart is simple — does the thing carry you towards depending on God, or towards depending on an object, a number, a person? Third, and this is the hardest sentence of all: there are two women in this chapter, one whom God remembered and one about whom nothing is recorded. God remembered Rachel, and yet Scripture gives us no promise that a child will certainly come. So please go on asking, and at the same time put the weight of your heart on the Lord who can give "I am enough" — because even when the child came, verse 24 says she immediately asked for the next one. A child cannot fill the hole in a human heart.
How do you bring a culture of comparison in a family or a church to a stop?

Three practical things. First, stop using ranking language: do not compare whose children, whose giving or whose ministry results in public. The tragedy of this chapter grew out of comparison. Second, make gifts and positions clear: comparison very often comes out of unclear roles — when people do not know what they count for, they confirm themselves by beating somebody else. Third, lead the way in giving thanks for the good of others: for a community to change its atmosphere somebody has to do it first, and do it in the open. And if you are a leader, there is one more thing to add: never use comparison to motivate people. It works in the short term, and in the long term it turns everyone into Rachel and Leah.
7. Living 321 Out — Let Go First, Then Wait for Him
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Jacob said, "Am I in God's place?" And in John 5:19 the Lord Jesus says, "Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing." Brothers and sisters, here is my role model: all his life he knew exactly what his position was, and he never once stepped past the Father. And when he said that sentence, he was not shrugging anything off. He was submitting.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter shows us that a perfectly correct sentence can be used out of an entirely wrong state of heart. "Am I in God's place?" is a shrug in chapter 30 and reverence in chapter 50. So the standard is not only whether the sentence is right; it also takes in where my heart is at the moment I say it.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice the way God guided Jacob. He did not stop him putting the rods into the trough; he told him afterwards, through a dream, "that was my doing." Brothers and sisters, God often lets the thing come off first and lets you learn afterwards that the real reason was him. On the day he pulls the curtain back, remember to say thank you, and do not argue.

Let Jesus be King — God remembered Rachel after every method of hers had run out. As long as there is still a method in your hand, you will never really open that hand. Letting Jesus be King means letting go first and waiting for him afterwards. And it is hard, because at the moment you let go, you are holding nothing at all.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — in verse 23 Rachel says, "God has taken away my reproach." After twenty-odd verses of sentences beginning with "I", at last there is one sentence whose subject is God. Glory going to God usually begins with a change of subject.

Establish God's system — the twelve tribes were born out of this very contest. Brothers and sisters, God did not go off and find himself a cleaner family. Establishing God's system begins inside the mess that already exists; it does not wait until everything is in order. If your family is not perfect, that is not a reason for not beginning — the twelve tribes had four mothers between them, and the kingdom of God walked out from there.

And here I want to say something honest to 321 itself. We talk a great deal about selflessness, and this chapter hands us a very important distinction: Rachel was not a selfish woman; she was simply in great pain. And a person in great pain automatically becomes self-centred — that is not a moral problem, it is what a wound does. So when you are shepherding someone who is in pain, do not begin by teaching them selflessness. What they need at that moment is to be seen and to be accompanied, and only after that to be brought to the God who can actually supply. To preach denying of self at a person who is still bleeding is to wound them a second time.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Contest
Brothers and sisters, one and the same family contest falls into four kinds of heart, and each one sees something different.

The proud heart says, "What a childish family." This heart finishes the chapter quite certain that it would never squabble over anything so petty. Brothers and sisters, ask yourself honestly: when was the last time you compared yourself with somebody on the inside? It may not have been children — it may have been a position, or whose opinion got taken up, or who got the credit. The scoreboard has changed its categories; the game is exactly the same.

The fearful heart says, "Am I also just working out my own methods?" This heart finishes the chapter and begins to doubt every effort it has ever made. To that heart I want to say this: the way to tell the difference is not to stop moving; it is to look at where your hope is placed. Jacob's problem was not that he took action; it was that he thought the action was the decisive thing. You may see a doctor, you may work hard, you may plan — as long as you know in your heart that the One who brings it about is God.

The ashamed heart says, "I am the one who never received." You may have been praying for years, watching other people receive one after another. Brothers and sisters, this chapter does not pretend that it does not hurt — it spends twenty-odd verses on that pain. And when verse 22 says "God remembered Rachel", the text offers no explanation of why it was at that moment. There are things whose reason we are not told. But that phrase, "God remembered", tells you this: he has not forgotten you, and he is counting the days.

The wounded heart says, "I am the one being asked." You may be the person who is always expected of and always drawn upon — parents wanting you to make something of yourself, a spouse wanting you to fill his emptiness, a child wanting you to prove your love. And however much you give, it is never enough. Brothers and sisters, what Jacob said was not wrong: "Am I in God's place?" You do not have to carry that seat, because you were never able to carry it in the first place. But notice where he went wrong — he said it and then walked away. The right thing to do is this: say the sentence that marks the boundary, and then go with that person to God.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, find your scoreboard. Write down who you most often compare yourself with, and what it is you compare. Then add one line beside it: who am I asking for approval in this?
Second, say the boundary sentence once. If somebody is asking you for something you cannot supply, say it gently this week, once: "I cannot give you this, but I can go with you to the One who can."
Third, change the subject. In your prayers this week, deliberately practise moving the subject of your sentences from "I want" to "God, you." That turn in verse 23 began with a change of subject.

Fourth, let go of one thing. Find something you are currently working hard to manage, and this week deliberately do nothing about it at all except pray. God remembered Rachel after the methods had run out.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: there is a woman in the Bible who said to her husband, "Give me children, or else I will die," and the husband answered, "Am I in God's place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"; afterwards the two sisters tried every remedy going, including a plant that folklore said would help a woman conceive, and the one who got the plant did not conceive while the one who gave it away did; and the Bible settles the whole ending in a single sentence — "God remembered Rachel."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer demand from a human being something that only God can give.
I declare that I will not stand in for God, and that I will not ask anybody else to stand in for God either.
I declare that I will let go first and wait for him afterwards; because while there is still a method in my hand, I will never really open that hand.
I declare that my system does not have to wait until everything is in order before it begins; God was already at work inside the mess.
This week I am supposed to "count what I already have", but honestly I feel I have nothing at all. What then?

Set the bar as low as it will go: it does not have to be an achievement, only something that is still there. A meal. One person who will still take your call. Today was not worse than yesterday. One part of your body that is still working properly. Write them down, three a day, for seven days. This is not making yourself feel better with words; it is pulling your eyes off the one gap and back to the whole field — Rachel's problem was not that she had nothing; it is that the one thing she did not have was all she could see. And if you have gone a long stretch feeling nothing good at all and unable to summon any energy for anything, please do not rely on a practice alone: go and talk to a pastor, and seek professional help as well.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, I want it to be the three words of verse 22:
Twenty-one whole verses, and every one of them human method: servants, mandrakes, bargaining, keeping score, naming, rivalry.
And then verse 22. One sentence. Three words.
Brothers and sisters, the structure of this chapter is itself the message. Human beings took twenty-one verses; God took one sentence.
And that "remembered" is the same word as "God remembered Noah" in chapter 8 — not the thought coming back, but the hand going to work.

And there is one more thing I want you to see. The eleven sons born into this household, together with Benjamin who came later, are the twelve tribes of Israel. And they were born into a family like this one: two sisters in competition, two servants used as instruments, a father who played favourites, and a heap of names used to keep score.
God did not go off and find himself a cleaner family.
He took this one, and with this one he established his kingdom.

And Judah, born in the middle of the rivalry, whose name means "praise", became the tribe of kings. And Joseph, asked for by his mother out of her deepest despair, went on to save the lives of the whole family.

The focus is not on whether I have received, not on who I have beaten in the comparison, and not on how far from perfect my family is. The focus is on Jesus — he came out of the bloodline of a household exactly like this one, and he became our King. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us: to open our hands once this week, and to hand that demand inside us back to the only One who can supply it. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of this lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ What Jacob said in answer to Rachel was theologically right, and it wounded her. What does right truth turn into when it is put in the wrong moment?
2. ★★ The "remembered" in "God remembered Rachel" means "to act because of a covenant". How does that definition help somebody who is waiting?
3. ★ The twelve tribes of Israel were born inside a family full of rivalry. What does that say to the idea that God only uses model families?
4. ★★ Jacob afterwards credited his prosperity to God and not to the rods. What warning does that give us about "spiritual methods"?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I am better than he is), fearful (I am going to be outdone), ashamed (I have nothing at all), wounded (I have been measured against other people since I was small). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Who do you most often compare yourself with? When did that comparison begin?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The gap inside me that never gets filled is …"
9. ★★ This week, in what way will you count three things every day that are "still there"? Say when in the day, and where you will write them down.

Leader's reminder: this lesson will touch wounds of infertility, of loss and of family comparison. Never say "if you have enough faith you will have one." If someone in the group is praying for a child or going through a loss, stay alongside them first, and follow them up privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there one comparing sentence you need to stop saying? Say that sentence out loud.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: in your group chat or at work, which kind of comparison most easily makes you uncomfortable?

12. ★★★ The practice of catching the feeling first: this week, when somebody pours out a trouble to you, begin by saying "I know how much this hurts", and hold the reasoning back until he asks you for it. Name the person you are likely to meet soon.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and this week send each other one thing that is "still there", every day. Say his name out loud now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there are two sisters in the Bible who competed with each other over bearing children, and the household was in chaos. Second, the twelve tribes of Israel came out of a family exactly like that. Third, so I believe that the place where God works does not have to be a model home.
